content:
At least, according to Texas Longhorns head coach Steve Sarkisian — who recently revealed a dilemma that coaches face whenever President Donald Trump decides to attend a game.

"One thing you have to be aware of when the president attends any event: every time he enters the field, leaves the field, or moves around inside the venue, all communications get cut," Sarkisian told reporters during a Zoom press conference on Thursday. "They cut your headsets. The coaches' headsets go down. The communication headsets between coaches and players all go down. So you have to have a contingency plan, no matter when it happens, and you won't get any warning. The signal just gets cut directly."

Sarkisian made these remarks before the Longhorns face the Tennessee Volunteers on Saturday at Neyland Stadium in Knoxville — a game Trump is expected to attend in person.

"You need to have a contingency plan in place, whether he walks in midway through the first quarter, leaves in the fourth quarter, or suddenly decides he needs to use the restroom — you have to be ready for it," Sarkisian continued, referring to the need to accommodate the president's various spur-of-the-moment whims. "You have to be prepared for the possibility that, at any moment, you lose all communications."

Later on Thursday, Sarkisian elaborated on the issue during an interview with "On Texas Football," citing an example he had heard from University of Miami coach Mario Cristobal.

"Mario Cristobal is a good friend of mine," he said. "Last year, when they played Indiana in the national championship, they had a drive late in the game."

"They had absolutely no communications because [Trump] left early, trying to get out before the game ended. So you don't get any warning. The signal just gets cut… so you have to be ready to handle that situation. This is really something unique, and it could happen at any point during this game."

The notion that Trump may have affected last season's championship game sent some college football fans into a frenzy.

Former "Meet the Press" host Chuck Todd wrote on X: "What the heck!!!?!? Are you saying Trump screwed up Miami's final drive? Is that what Sark is implying? I stopped following sports news for a while after Miami lost that game, but was this widely reported at the time?"

Sports reporter Alex Donno posted on X: "You're not serious, right?? They cut their communications without any warning during Miami's final drive in the championship game, when they were down by 6??"

In the story Sarkisian told, the dramatic timing of the communications being cut has been denied and downplayed by parties involved with both teams.

An anonymous source on Miami's 2025 coaching staff told The Athletic that "the incident occurred before the final drive." Indiana's Curt Cignetti told ESPN that the headsets lost signal with about 6:45 remaining, when Miami had the ball.

Cignetti told ESPN: "The signal came back before the snap. After that, both teams had communications restored."

CBS Sports also spoke with multiple sources from the Miami team about the communications failure. Two sources told CBS that the outage did not occur during the final drive. All sources said with "high confidence" that the outage lasted only "a few plays" and "had no noticeable impact on the outcome of the game."

Whether or not Trump actually hurt Miami, some sports fans believe the president's attendance at major sporting events brings bad luck — especially to teams he favors.

The notion of a "Trump curse" has spread widely on social media in the context of sports, reportedly originating from the president allegedly "putting a hex" on the New York Knicks during Game 3 of the NBA Finals, as well as the U.S. team losing to Belgium at the World Cup — even though Trump had actively cheered for the U.S. team. Earlier, New York Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart — who had introduced Trump at a rally in May — suffered a knee injury during Monday's game against the Los Angeles Rams, requiring surgery and ruling him out for the remainder of the regular season.

Many others have extended the "Trump curse" narrative to cover virtually anything the president has touched — such as the demolition of the White House East Wing, the chaotic Reflecting Pool renovation project, the pathetically low attendance at the Great American State Fair he attended… or, going further still, to describe the overall state of America at present.
